# Education Systems Overview
## Middle East, Africa, and South Asia
Israel enforces compulsory education from kindergarten through 12th grade across diverse tracks—including secular, religious, Haredi, and Arab sector schools—alongside private and integrated Jewish-Arab options promoting coexistence. Despite legal protections, underserved minorities face disparities, though affirmative action has boosted STEM and university access. The high school matriculation exam (Bagrut) is pivotal, with tertiary attainment surpassing OECD averages despite challenges like large classes and gender dropout gaps. Egypt’s centrally governed system balances a rich educational legacy with modern basic, secondary, and tertiary levels, but struggles with unequal access, poor primary education quality, heavy reliance on private tutoring, and high unemployment, especially among women. Nigeria offers six years each of primary and secondary education leading to university through various routes but contends with funding shortages, infrastructure deficits, insecurity, regional disparities, and significant barriers to female education. Sri Lanka features a multi-religious education system serving over 4 million students across public, private, elite, and monastic schools; free yet highly competitive state universities fuel a large private tuition sector amid calls for reform. Indonesia mandates 12 years of education across primary and secondary levels with secular, religious (notably pesantren), and special needs schools, guided by curricular diversification and a national qualification framework, though funding and teacher distribution challenges persist.

# Education Systems Overview
## East Asia and Europe
Taiwan requires 12 years of compulsory education emphasizing Mandarin, math, science, English, and arts, offering academic and vocational tracks preparing students for higher education modeled on the U.S. system. Its universities attract international students, and discipline is stressed, though corporal punishment persists unofficially. Armenia mandates 12 years focused on Armenian language and culture while promoting multilingualism and aligning higher education with European standards like Bologna and Erasmus+, addressing dropout rates with non-formal education initiatives. Iran’s centralized system provides mandatory education through lower secondary and free or subsidized higher education, blending modernization with mandatory religious content and employing competitive entrance exams that favor STEM and female enrollment. Norway offers inclusive elementary through upper secondary education with academic and vocational tracks, flexible entry to higher education, and strong emphasis on special education, ICT, and public funding.
Turkey’s 12-year compulsory system includes primary, middle, and secondary phases with general, vocational, and technical tracks. It has over 160 universities, many with ABET accreditation, supports minority languages, and participates in Erasmus despite political constraints on university governance. Sweden features an inclusive education system beginning with play-based preschool and nine years of compulsory schooling, followed by a three-year gymnasieskola offering varied academic and vocational paths, including Sámi and adult education. Higher education complies with Bologna standards and is largely tuition-free for residents, complemented by a sizeable independent school sector focused on equality, though international assessment outcomes vary.

# Education Systems Overview
## Western Europe
France operates a secular, centralized system mandating schooling from ages 3 to 18, with public and private options including state-contracted and fully independent religious schools. Early childhood education focuses on literacy and numeracy, leading to secondary education culminating in the baccalauréat or vocational diplomas. The Grandes Écoles select top students via competitive preparatory classes and charge higher fees, contrasting with heavily subsidized public universities. The system emphasizes tolerance by excluding religious instruction and banning prominent religious symbols, with strict homeschooling regulations and over 100 international schools offering diverse curricula. Vocational training complements academic tracks, and the Bologna framework facilitates credit transfer and professional education.
England’s education mandates schooling from ages 5 to 18, structured into Key Stages culminating in GCSEs, with diverse post-16 academic and vocational pathways such as A-levels and T Levels incorporating industry placements. Approximately 93% attend state-funded schools, including Academies and selective Grammar schools; independent schools enroll the remainder. The National Curriculum promotes core subjects and personal development, supplemented by extracurriculars and welfare programs. Higher education offers three-year degrees and postgraduate options with capped tuition fees and financial aid, attracting significant international enrollment.

# Education Systems Overview
## Asia-Pacific
Hong Kong’s education system spans kindergarten to senior secondary education, with compulsory schooling up to age 18. It balances broad foundational learning and specialization, culminating mainly in the HKDSE exam, while also offering alternatives like the International Baccalaureate. Schools vary from government to private and international, primarily delivering instruction in English but increasingly promoting Cantonese and Putonghua. Recent reforms emphasize patriotism aligned with national security goals amid enrollment declines and teacher emigration. Vocational, adult, and special education sectors receive substantial support, with plans to integrate AI and strengthen ties to the Greater Bay Area.

# Education Systems Overview
## Sub-Saharan Africa
Ghana offers about 20 years of education from kindergarten through undergraduate levels, conducted in English with free and compulsory basic education for ages 4–15. Senior high school provides academic and vocational tracks completed via national exams. Despite rapid tertiary expansion, vocational education remains informal and underdeveloped, hampered by infrastructure challenges and weak industry ties. Education consumes a significant portion of the national budget but depends heavily on private sector involvement and decentralized governance. Literacy and equity have improved, though female and rural student representation in tertiary education remains low. ICT policies aim to elevate quality but face implementation hurdles alongside a growing network of international schools.
